facts.statement: The study used 100 C57BL/6 mice that were randomly divided into five groups of 20 animals each: a sham group, a spinal cord injury group, and three groups receiving low, medium, or high doses of hesperidin.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Hesperidin was given to the mice by mouth once a day for 21 days, starting two hours after the spinal cord injury.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: By day 21, only the group receiving the highest dose of hesperidin showed a statistically significant improvement in motor and sensory function, while the lower doses did not reach statistical significance.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: In spinal cord tissue taken on day 7, the high-dose hesperidin group had lower levels of the pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-α and higher levels of anti-inflammatory cytokines compared to the injury-only group.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The high-dose hesperidin group showed lower levels of the oxidative stress marker MDA and higher activities of the antioxidant enzymes SOD, GSH-Px, and CAT compared to the spinal cord injury group.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: Hesperidin treatment was associated with fewer activated microglia cells and reduced phosphorylation of the signaling proteins ERK1/2 and JNK, while the total amounts of these proteins remained unchanged.
facts.subject: animals

facts.statement: The authors note that further experiments are needed to prove that hesperidin directly causes the observed improvements, rather than just being associated with them.
facts.subject: animals
